editorial.headline: Non-Hazardous Waste Collection: Open Nationally, Blocked In Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers local collection of non-hazardous waste and recyclables, open nationally to foreign ownership yet blocked for PT PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 38110 is the business of collecting non-hazardous waste at the local level. Its centre of gravity is practical, municipal, and operational: household and business waste gathered through bins, containers, and similar systems; recyclable materials whether already separated or not; non-hazardous waste from animal or plant sources; used cooking oil and fats; rubbish from public places; construction and demolition waste; rubble and debris; factory waste; and the operation of transfer facilities for non-hazardous waste. The scope is collection and transfer, not wastewater, hazardous waste, permanent disposal or storage, or the operation of sorting facilities for recoverable materials.

The record also gives this activity a distinctly community-enterprise profile. It is open at Mikro, Kecil, and Menengah scales, and the Indonesian scope names Bank Sampah Induk, entrepreneurs, self-employed operators, and sociopreneurs as actors, including conventional businesses and digital-platform models. In plain English, this is the code for the front line of non-hazardous waste logistics: the people and systems that aggregate waste before later processing, disposal, or recovery happens elsewhere. It can be small, local, and service-led, but it can also sit inside a more organised platform or social-enterprise model, provided the activity remains within the collection scope.

Nationally, the investment signal is straightforward. The record marks the activity as TERBUKA and gives a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That means the national position shown here is open to foreign ownership up to the full recorded ceiling. There is no lower national cap in this slim record, and no separate national condition should be read into it. For a founder reading only the national line, this looks like a clean opening for a foreign-owned structure.

Bali changes the practical answer. The Bali status is Closed to PMA (no Besar scale), and the record states that PMA registration is blocked because OSS has no Usaha Besar scale row for this activity, leaving it reserved for UMKM; a PT PMA is treated as Usaha Besar by law and therefore cannot register it. The Bali moratorium adds a second, broader barrier: Bali blocks Low and Medium-Low risk PMA registration island-wide on a permanent basis under the cited governor letter. So the honest reading is narrow but important: nationally this activity is foreign-open up to 100%, but a foreigner cannot register it as a PT PMA in Bali today.
